newsitem.title: UK: Bond boutique welcomes Dresdner embrace.
newsitem.headline: Bond boutique welcomes Dresdner embrace.

text.p: Another innovative British financial boutique, Luthy Baillie Dowsett Pethick & Co, was snapped up by a European banking giant on Tuesday, as one of the founders of the Eurobond specialist boutique welcomed the takeover by Dresdner Bank AG as being at "a fair price."

Peter Luthy, a 45-year-old American, one of four key players who founded the company in 1990, told Reuters he could not disclose what Dresdner Kleinwort Benson (Dresdner's investment banking arm) was paying for the 15-person team, or what individuals would gain.

But Luthy said it was not nearly of the same magnitude as NatWest Market's much discussed takeover last week of corporate finance boutique Hambro Magan for a sum analysts said was around 80 million pounds ($126.6 million).
"The original investment in our equity has done quite well," he said, adding that 13 of Luthy Baillie's employees held equity totalling just over half of the company's total shares.
"They (Dresdner) are paying a fair price. It's a business which has made money in all of its six years," he said adding it was a strategic sale rather than a forced sale.
"We are committed body, mind and soul (to the venture)," he said, acknowledging there were employment contracts and stressing Dresdner was buying an ongoing business.

Dresdner, Germany's second largest commercial bank, said it was buying the firm as part of a shift in its Eurobond operations to London. Under the arrangements Luthy and fellow founder Jan Pethick will take on global responsibility for the group's primary and secondary Eurobond business.

Luthy set up and managed the financing department at Lehman Brothers in the 1980s and also worked with Dresdner board member Hans-Georg Hoffman there. Some Eurobond dealers suggested this may have been a factor in the move.
"He's a very bright and charismatic guy. He's a hands-on Eurobond man," said one.

Luthy said his company's reliance on the secondary market, where bonds are traded rather than issued, had meant it was constrained in the staff it could attract and had also been adversely hit by recent changes in the market.

"We learned a hell of a lot. But our business skills are better used in a big firm. The opportunities are better in a big firm," said Luthy, who started his career as a bond salesman in New York in 1977.

The new operation should be up and running by November and will make use of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson's existing strengths as well as Luthy Baillie's focus on "...the 200 largest institutional clients in the world."

"We're just another peg in the global business of the group," Luthy said, adding that his firm had been approached by others, including some bigger offers, but had only recently come to a decision that it would not continue to "go it alone."
Luthy said he hopes to maintain the relationship his firm has built up with these clients, providing them with research analysis on the timing and credit selection of bond-buying.
"Kleinwort is a very conservative player in the market so Luthy Baillie will take them into areas they have not got the expertise to cover," one Eurobond trader said.

One commentator said Luthy Bailllie's performance over its six-year lifespan had been mixed, but that the firm had managed to maintain a client base throughout and provide a useful service despite its small size.
